title: When should you choose Kafka over Solace — when you need durable event streaming, long-term replay, event sourcing, Kafka Streams/ksqlDB ecosystem, and partitioned log scalability — and when should you choose Solace — when consumers have diverse and changing routing needs, you want broker-native hierarchical subscription, and you need dynamic topic filtering without creating new topics?
shortTitle: When should you choose Kafka over Solace, and when should you choose Solace over Kafka?

s1_definition.profdef: The choice between Kafka and Solace is a choice between two different core models. Kafka is a durable, partitioned, append-only log that excels at long-term retention, deterministic replay, event sourcing, and a rich stream-processing ecosystem through Kafka Streams and ksqlDB, scaling horizontally by partition. Solace PubSub+ is a broker-centric message router whose strength is broker-native hierarchical topic routing with wildcard subscriptions, letting consumers with diverse and changing routing needs filter dynamically without anyone creating new topics. You choose Kafka when the dominant requirement is durable streaming, replay, and stream processing; you choose Solace when the dominant requirement is flexible, broker-side, content-shaped routing to many heterogeneous consumers.
s1_definition.analogy: Think of Kafka as National Bank of India's permanent ledger vault: every transaction is written down in order and kept for years so you can replay the exact history, rebuild any report, and feed analytics. Think of Solace as the bank's smart internal mail room: it does not keep letters forever, but it is brilliant at instantly sorting each letter to exactly the desks that asked for that kind of letter, even as desks keep changing what they want. If your need is "remember everything and replay it", you want the vault. If your need is "deliver the right slice to the right desk right now, and the desks keep changing", you want the mail room.
s1_definition.oneliner: Choose Kafka when you must store and replay the event history; choose Solace when you must route live events flexibly to ever-changing consumers.
s1_definition.raw:
**Professional definition:** The choice between Kafka and Solace is a choice between two different core models. Kafka is a durable, partitioned, append-only log that excels at long-term retention, deterministic replay, event sourcing, and a rich stream-processing ecosystem through Kafka Streams and ksqlDB, scaling horizontally by partition. Solace PubSub+ is a broker-centric message router whose strength is broker-native hierarchical topic routing with wildcard subscriptions, letting consumers with diverse and changing routing needs filter dynamically without anyone creating new topics. You choose Kafka when the dominant requirement is durable streaming, replay, and stream processing; you choose Solace when the dominant requirement is flexible, broker-side, content-shaped routing to many heterogeneous consumers.

**In simple words (banking analogy):** Think of Kafka as National Bank of India's permanent ledger vault: every transaction is written down in order and kept for years so you can replay the exact history, rebuild any report, and feed analytics. Think of Solace as the bank's smart internal mail room: it does not keep letters forever, but it is brilliant at instantly sorting each letter to exactly the desks that asked for that kind of letter, even as desks keep changing what they want. If your need is "remember everything and replay it", you want the vault. If your need is "deliver the right slice to the right desk right now, and the desks keep changing", you want the mail room.

**One line to remember:** Choose Kafka when you must store and replay the event history; choose Solace when you must route live events flexibly to ever-changing consumers.

sections.s2_technical:
Kafka's defining property is the durable log. Records are appended to partitions and retained for a configured time or size, often days, weeks, or indefinitely with compaction. Because the log persists and each consumer tracks its own offset, a consumer can rewind and replay from any point. This is what makes event sourcing possible: the log of events is the source of truth, and you can rebuild state by replaying. For example, a settlement service can reset a consumer group's offset to the start of the `trade.events` topic and recompute every position, which you would express operationally with `kafka-consumer-groups.sh --reset-offsets --to-earliest --execute`. Solace is a messaging broker whose persistence and replay model is different and generally not aimed at long-horizon reprocessing of an entire history.

Kafka's second property is the stream-processing ecosystem. Kafka Streams lets you write a topology in the application that reads a topic, does joins, windowed aggregations, and stateful transforms, and writes results back to Kafka, all with exactly-once semantics. ksqlDB lets you express the same with SQL. For instance, a fraud service can use a Kafka Streams aggregation over a five-minute hopping window to count transactions per account and flag spikes. Solace does not offer this native streaming-compute ecosystem; you would pair it with an external processor.

Kafka's third property is partitioned horizontal scale with ordering. A topic is split into partitions, each an ordered log, and ordering is guaranteed within a partition keyed by, for example, account id, so all events for one account stay ordered while the topic as a whole scales across brokers and consumers. This gives very high sequential throughput, which is why banks use Kafka as the firm-wide event backbone.

Solace's defining property is broker-native hierarchical routing. The broker understands structured topic strings and wildcard subscriptions and does the matching itself, so a consumer with a specific or changing interest just adjusts its subscription pattern and immediately receives exactly the matching slice, without anyone creating a topic. This is the right tool when you have many heterogeneous consumers whose routing needs are diverse and keep changing, such as trading desks each wanting a different cut of a market feed. Solace also supports multiple delivery models including direct low-latency fan-out and persistent queues, and multi-protocol access such as JMS, MQTT, AMQP, and REST, which matters in mixed enterprise estates.

So the decision rules are as follows. Choose Kafka when you need durable event streaming kept for a long time, deterministic replay, event sourcing where the log is the source of truth, the Kafka Streams or ksqlDB processing ecosystem, and partitioned log scalability with per-key ordering at very high throughput. Choose Solace when consumers have diverse and frequently changing routing needs, when you want the broker itself to do hierarchical, content-shaped routing with wildcards, when you need dynamic filtering without creating new topics (avoiding topic proliferation), and when low-latency fan-out and multi-protocol access to many consumers matter more than long-term replay.

The senior nuance is that these are not mutually exclusive and are frequently complementary. A common bank architecture uses Solace for real-time, finely routed, low-latency distribution to desks and uses Kafka as the durable, replayable backbone for retention, analytics, and event sourcing, sometimes bridging the two so an event flows through Solace for live routing and lands in Kafka for history. The wrong move is to force one tool into the other's job: forcing Kafka to route finely causes topic proliferation, and forcing Solace to be your seven-year replayable ledger fights its design.
sections.s3_banking:
National Bank of India must handle two very different requirements for its trade and transaction events, and the team must pick the right tool for each.

Problem 1 — Compliance requires that every trade event be stored for seven years and be replayable, so that at any time the settlement ledger can be rebuilt by replaying the full history from the beginning. This is exactly what Kafka's durable, offset-based log gives you: retain forever, reset offsets, and replay to reconstruct state, which is the essence of event sourcing.

Problem 2 — Multiple trading desks each want a different, frequently changing slice of the live market and transaction feed, and they must not wait for a platform team to create a new topic every time their interest changes. This is exactly what Solace's broker-native hierarchical routing gives you: each desk sets a wildcard subscription and the broker delivers the matching slice instantly, with no topic creation.

Problem 3 — The architecture team wants a decision helper that, given a requirement's characteristics, recommends Kafka or Solace with a clear reason, so that engineers stop forcing the wrong tool and causing either topic proliferation or a broken replay story.

The demo models this with a small decision engine. A `Requirement` carries flags such as needsLongReplay, needsStreamProcessing, needsFlexibleRouting, and routingChangesOften. A `BrokerAdvisor` applies the decision rules and returns a recommendation with a reason. The `main` method runs the compliance-replay requirement and the changing-desk-routing requirement through the advisor and prints the recommendation, then shows a tiny illustration of Kafka replay (offset reset) and Solace dynamic subscription (pattern change) to make the trade-off concrete.

##### 4c. Configuration File

```yaml
# application.yml
spring:
  application:
    name: broker-choice-advisor
kafka:
  bootstrap-servers: kafka-1:9092
  retention: 7y          # long-term replay for event sourcing
solace:
  msgVpn: desks-vpn       # dynamic subscriptions, no topic creation
```

```bash
# Kafka replay in reality (rebuild ledger by replaying history):

```

##### 4f. Logging notes

The advisor logs its scoring at `fine` and the final recommendation at `info`, so you can both see the decision and, when needed, the reason it scored durability or routing as dominant.
sections.s5_journey:
Input data: two requirements, one for seven-year compliance replay with stream processing, one for many trading desks whose routing changes often.

Step 1: The compliance requirement enters the advisor with needsLongReplay and needsStreamProcessing both true. The advisor's first rule checks durability and replay; both are set, so it scores durability as dominant.

Step 2: The advisor returns a recommendation of Kafka, with the reason that a durable partitioned log gives long-term retention, deterministic replay, event sourcing, and the Kafka Streams and ksqlDB ecosystem with per-key ordering. This is logged at info.

Step 3: The desks requirement enters the advisor with needsFlexibleRouting and routingChangesOften both true, and the durability flags false. The first rule does not fire because durability is not needed.

Step 4: The second rule checks flexible or changing routing; both are set, so it scores routing as dominant and returns a recommendation of Solace, with the reason that broker-native hierarchical wildcard subscriptions let diverse, changing consumers filter dynamically with no new topics.

Step 5: The demo prints two concrete illustrations. For Kafka it shows that rebuilding the ledger means resetting the trade.events consumer group to the earliest offset and recomputing, which only a durable replayable log can do. For Solace it shows a desk changing its subscription live from a narrow pattern to a broad multi-level wildcard, receiving a different slice immediately with no topic creation.

```
23:14:51 INFO    REQ[7yr trade replay / event sourcing] -> CHOOSE KAFKA BECAUSE durable partitioned log gives long-term retention, deterministic replay, event sourcing, and the Kafka Streams/ksqlDB ecosystem with per-key ordering
23:14:51 INFO    REQ[Trading desks, diverse changing slices] -> CHOOSE SOLACE BECAUSE broker-native hierarchical wildcard subscriptions let diverse, changing consumers filter dynamically with no new topics (no topic proliferation)
23:14:51 INFO    KAFKA replay example: reset trade.events group to earliest and recompute ledger
23:14:51 INFO    SOLACE dynamic routing example: Rajesh's desk changes subscription live
```

sections.s6_takeaway:
The choice between Kafka and Solace comes down to which core model your dominant requirement needs. Kafka is a durable, partitioned, append-only log, so you choose it when you need long-term event retention, deterministic replay, event sourcing where the log is the source of truth, the Kafka Streams and ksqlDB stream-processing ecosystem, and partitioned horizontal scalability with per-key ordering at very high throughput. Because each consumer tracks its own offset against a retained log, you can rewind and replay history to rebuild state, which is exactly what event sourcing and firm-wide analytics depend on.

Solace PubSub+ is a broker-centric message router whose defining strength is broker-native hierarchical routing with wildcard subscriptions. You choose Solace when consumers have diverse and frequently changing routing needs, when you want the broker itself to do content-shaped hierarchical routing, and when you need dynamic filtering without creating new topics, which avoids the topic proliferation that Kafka suffers when routing dimensions multiply. Solace also shines for low-latency fan-out to many heterogeneous consumers and for multi-protocol access such as JMS, MQTT, AMQP, and REST in mixed enterprise estates.

The key senior insight is that these are not competitors forced into one slot; they are usually complementary. A common bank architecture uses Solace for the real-time, finely routed, low-latency distribution of market and transaction feeds to trading desks whose interests keep changing, while Kafka acts as the durable, replayable backbone that retains every event for years for compliance, analytics, and event sourcing. Events can flow through Solace for live routing and land in Kafka for history, so each tool does the job its design is best at.

At National Bank of India I applied exactly this split. Compliance needed seven-year trade retention and the ability to rebuild the settlement ledger by replaying the whole history, so that went to Kafka, where we could reset a consumer group to the earliest offset and recompute. Meanwhile many trading desks each wanted a different and often-changing slice of the live feed and could not wait for a platform team to create a topic each time, so that went to Solace, where each desk simply adjusted its wildcard subscription and received the new slice instantly. The mistake I always warn against is forcing one tool into the other's role: pushing fine routing onto Kafka explodes topic counts, and making Solace your long-horizon replayable ledger fights its design, so I match the tool to the dominant requirement and let them work together.
